title: Dolphin Groups & Population Structure
text:
Sightings vs. Unique Individual Dolphins
A crucial distinction in marine mammal science separates sighting events from unique individuals:

2,206 visual sightings (2021–2026) represent distinct encounter events—the same resident dolphin in Sarasota Bay can be photographed dozens of times across seasons.
Within those 2,206 sightings, 259 records explicitly counted total group size (individualCount), summing to 1,749 individual dolphin observations, with a median pod of 4 dolphins and a mean of 6.75 dolphins (ranging from solitary foragers up to 44 dolphins). The remaining 1,947 records verified presence without recording a full headcount and are left as NA rather than assumed to be 1.
Long-term dorsal-fin photo-identification by Wells et al. (2025) tracks 482 uniquely cataloged resident Sarasota Bay dolphins over five decades (~160–170 core residents alive in any single year).

title: Where Do Sightings Concentrate in Sarasota Bay?
text:
Mapping all 207 verified sightings inside the Sarasota Bay study boundary (2021–2026) reveals that observations do not spread evenly across open bay waters. Instead, sightings cluster tightly at narrow tidal bottlenecks connecting the bay to the Gulf of Mexico: Anna Maria Sound and Palma Sola Causeway in the north, Longboat Pass, New Pass and City Island (Mote Marine Laboratory), Big Sarasota Pass, and Venice Inlet in the south. Comparing the first half of our window (2021–2023, 96 sightings) against the second half (2024–2026, 111 sightings) shows that these same five coastal corridors persist across both periods.









Part of this clustering is genuinely ecological. Tidal inlets like Big Sarasota Pass and Venice Inlet funnel strong currents between seagrass flats and nearshore Gulf reefs, concentrating mullet, pinfish, and seatrout into predictable foraging lanes where dolphins ambush prey. Meanwhile, protected interior embayments like Palma Sola Bay and Roberts Bay offer shallow seagrass beds (1–3 m depth) that shelter mothers and calves from open-water bull sharks.
Just as importantly, however, spatial heatmaps of citizen-contributed sightings reflect human shoreline access. Causeways, fishing piers, public beaches, and kayak launches sit directly beside Anna Maria Sound, City Island, Ringling Causeway, and Venice Jetty—giving observers unobstructed vantage points without needing a research vessel. Open-water stretches in the middle of Sarasota Bay show fewer grid detections not because dolphins avoid them, but because systematic boat transects (like SDRP’s monthly photo-ID surveys) are required to sample mid-bay waters evenly.

title: When Are Dolphins Most Present in Sarasota Bay?
text:
Across six years of recent observations (2021–2026), recorded visual sightings in Sarasota Bay follow a sharp two-peak seasonal curve—and an equally striking late-summer trough. Sightings surge in January (30) and March (34) during Florida’s dry winter–spring boating season, rebound in June (21) and July (24), and then plummet by more than two-thirds during August (8), September (7), and October (8). Plotting Sarasota Bay alongside all 2,206 statewide coastal sightings reveals the exact same rhythm across Florida: spring (March–April) accounts for over 28% of all annual sightings, while August through November consistently marks the lowest recorded totals of the year.









If we interpreted raw sighting counts literally, we might conclude that bottlenose dolphins migrate out of Sarasota Bay every August. Five decades of systematic photo-identification and tagging by the Sarasota Dolphin Research Program prove the exact opposite. In their landmark analysis of 482 resident Sarasota Bay dolphins, Wells et al. (2025) demonstrate that Sarasota Bay supports a year-round resident community with virtually zero seasonal turnover (annual immigration of just 0.003–0.013). Even more remarkably, 81% of Sarasota Bay dolphin births occur between May and July, meaning mothers and newborn calves are most concentrated in warm, shallow bay nursery meadows during late summer and early autumn.
Why, then, do 2021–2026 visual records drop every August–October? Because opportunistic visual databases measure when people are on the water, not just when dolphins are present. March coincides with peak tourism and calm dry-season seas, whereas August through October brings extreme Gulf heat, daily afternoon lightning storms, red-tide blooms, and peak tropical cyclone activity—driving boaters and shoreline photographers indoors while resident dolphins remain below the surface. Passive underwater hydrophones in the Sarasota Bay Listening Network record continuous dolphin whistle activity right through those stormy late-summer months, underscoring why visual effort must always be separated from biological presence.

title: How Has Recorded Dolphin Presence Changed From 2021–2026?
text:
Between 2021 and 2026, annual verified dolphin sightings rose across both Sarasota Bay and the surrounding central Gulf Coast (Greater Suncoast, spanning Tampa Bay, Sarasota Bay, and Charlotte Harbor). Inside Sarasota Bay, annual sightings climbed from 25 in 2021 and 32 in 2022 to 39 in 2023, dipped to 32 in 2024, and rebounded to 41 in 2025 and 38 through mid-November 2026. Across the broader Suncoast estuaries, sightings nearly doubled from 98 in 2021 to 176 in 2025 and 179 in 2026 (even before December 2026 has elapsed).









Crucially, rising annual sighting totals from 2021 to 2026 do not prove that Sarasota Bay’s dolphin population grew. Instead, upward long-term trends in GBIF/iNaturalist records primarily reflect expanding smartphone wildlife photography and increased post-2021 outdoor recreation. Meanwhile, the sharp autumn dips—especially Q3–Q4 2024, when Hurricanes Debby, Helene, and Milton made back-to-back impacts along Sarasota Bay, damaging marinas, piers, and barrier islands—illustrate how severe weather temporarily halts coastal observation effort.
Long-term demographic studies provide the true biological baseline behind these fluctuations. Wells et al. (2025) report a mean annual birth rate of 0.071 balanced against a mean annual maximum loss rate of 0.072, showing that Sarasota Bay’s resident community remains remarkably stable from year to year—and historically stays inside its home range even through major hurricanes, while elevated loss episodes typically trace to severe Karenia brevis red-tide blooms and prey depletion rather than wind events alone.

title: Time-of-Day Activity Explorer (2021–2026)
text:
Out of 2,206 sightings in our 2021–2026 dataset, 2,101 records (95.2%) include an exact local clock timestamp (105 records reported only the date and are excluded below rather than assigned an artificial hour).

Critical methodological note on effort: Visual sightings require daylight and human observers on boats, piers, or beaches. Sharp drop-offs after sunset reflect visual observer effort, not dolphins sleeping or leaving Sarasota Bay—passive acoustic studies using the Sarasota Bay Listening Network show that dolphins vocalize and forage actively throughout the night.

title: Scientific Context, Data Sources & Methodology
text:
Sarasota Bay is a shallow, 56-mile coastal lagoon system along Florida’s central Gulf Coast, sheltered by barrier islands (Anna Maria Island, Longboat Key, Lido Key, Siesta Key, and Casey Key) and carpeted with seagrass meadows, mangrove fringes, oyster bars, and tidal passes. Since 1970, the Sarasota Dolphin Research Program (SDRP)—a partnership of Brookfield Zoo Chicago and Mote Marine Laboratory—has maintained the world’s longest-running study of a wild cetacean community.

Dorsal-Fin Photo-Identification & FinBase: Every adult bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) acquires distinctive nicks and notches along the trailing edge of its dorsal fin. SDRP conducts monthly boat-based photo-ID surveys and catalogs individual life histories in FinBase, tracking five generations of multi-decade residents.
Demographic & Life-History Findings (Wells et al., 2025): Across 482 resident individuals, females live up to 67 years (males 52 years), give birth mainly in May–July (81% of births) at an average 3.5-year interval, and show near-zero immigration (0.003–0.013/year).
Acoustic Monitoring & Signature Whistles (SBLN): Because murky estuarine water and nighttime darkness limit visual sightings, SDRP and collaborators operate the Sarasota Bay Listening Network (SBLN / PALS Network)—shore-based underwater hydrophones that continuously detect echolocation clicks and individualized signature whistles used by mothers and calves to maintain contact.
Environmental & Human Pressures: Peer-reviewed SDRP research identifies Karenia brevis harmful algal blooms (red tide), recreational boat strikes, fishing-gear entanglement/ingestion, and seagrass habitat loss as the primary threats affecting resident survival.

title: Scientific Context, Data Sources & Methodology
text:
3. Geographic Boundaries, Cleaning & Missing Data

Study Boundaries: Because Sarasota Bay alone contains 207 public visual sightings for 2021–2026, the dataset encompasses Florida coastal waters (24.4°N–31.0°N, 87.6°W–79.8°W; n = 2,206) while explicitly isolating the Sarasota Bay Study Area (26.85°N–27.56°N, 82.85°W–82.30°W; n = 207)—matching SDRP’s Anna Maria Sound to Venice/Lemon Bay corridor—and adjacent Tampa Bay & Charlotte Harbor (26.40°N–28.20°N, 83.20°W–82.00°W; n = 680).
Deduplication: Records were deduplicated on unique gbif_id (2,206 unique occurrences across 1,110 distinct calendar dates).
Documented Missing Values (Never Imputed):

December 2026: Marked Unavailable (NA) across all 72-month charts because data were retrieved on November 13, 2026.
Clock Timestamps: Present in 2,101 of 2,206 records (95.2%); the 105 date-only records are excluded from hourly analyses rather than assigned a default hour.
Pod Size (group_size): Explicitly reported in 259 of 2,206 records (11.7%); the remaining 1,947 presence-only records are stored as NA rather than assumed to be 1.

title: Scientific Context, Data Sources & Methodology
text:
4. Methodological Limitations & Biases

Visual Effort Bias: Citizen-science sightings depend on fair weather, daylight, and shoreline/boater access. Lower counts at night, in mid-bay open water, or during August–October hurricane months reflect reduced human observation effort, not dolphin absence.
Acoustic vs. Visual Metrics: Acoustic hydrophone detections measure vocal activity rate within a station’s listening radius (~500–1,500 m)—a single whistling pod can trigger hundreds of detections per hour, whereas silent foraging dolphins go undetected acoustically. Visual sightings and acoustic detections therefore measure complementary dimensions of presence and are never merged into a single raw count.
Sightings vs. Abundance: Repeated sightings of long-lived resident dolphins over time cannot be summed to estimate population size without formal mark–recapture photo-identification modeling.
